# SWOS Reverse Engineering (RE) Project

## Introduction

I began reverse-engineering the Amiga version of Sensible World of Soccer (SWOS) in August 2025. My goal is to produce a faithful, well-documented understanding of the original game's codebase and data formats so that bugs can be analyzed, features can be studied, and future ports or tooling can build on a solid foundation. Although the target is the Amiga build, this work stands on the shoulders of prior DOS research - most notably Zlatko Karakas (@zlatkok), whose IDA Pro database of the DOS version provided a treasure trove of function/variable names, comments, and structures that I carefully adapted to the Amiga binary.

The workflow blends IDA Pro for disassembly with Ghidra for decompilation. While IDA excels at organizing symbols and navigation, only Ghidra currently offers a practical m68k to C decompiler, so I import the IDA database into Ghidra using the community plugin. To make this round-trip smoother and the output more accurate, I modified that plugin to improve export fidelity and symbol transfer. From there, I rely on a suite of custom Python scripts to lift the overall quality of the decompilation: normalizing calling conventions, taming aggressive casts, teasing apart union-like data access, and annotating engine-specific patterns that recur throughout the code.

Automated decompilation can only take you so far. SWOS - like many performance-tuned 90s games - leans on tight register juggling, overlapping data layouts, and hand-written assembly tricks that don't cleanly map to high-level constructs. After a certain point, manual reconstruction becomes essential: refactoring control flow into meaningful functions, elevating magic numbers into enums and constants, and reconciling ambiguous pointer arithmetic with real engine abstractions.

Looking ahead, I plan to use AI-assisted cleanup to accelerate the most tedious parts of this process - e.g., proposing types for "undefined" temporaries, surfacing likely structure fields, and suggesting clearer function boundaries - while keeping a human in the loop for all correctness and style decisions. The aim isn't to auto-port the game, but to produce readable, reviewable C that reflects the original intent of the Amiga code, informed by DOS symbols where appropriate and verified against observed behavior.

## DOS Version

```
PC version of SWOS was written as a conversion from Amiga. It can be deduced by analyzing the code, and there are even some left over strings such as `INSERT BLANK DISK IN DF0:`. There are 15 memory locations (dwords) that are used as registers. Their start is at 0x3146d. These dwords correspond to Amiga s MC68000 processor registers: data registers D0-D7 and address registers A0-A7

This is not a mistake (15 locations for 16 registers) because register A7 (stack pointer) is mapped directly to Intel's esp register. This means that PC version of SWOS is using so called static emulation, where whole program is translated into host machine language and then executed. Other type of emulation is dynamic emulation, where an interpreter is used that interprets original code run-time (this is the way most emulators operate).

Since SWOS is a commercial game, it was more feasibile to use the first approach. I think they did the following: first Amiga s source code (which I believe was mostly written in assembler, or some optimizing C compiler - somebody correct me if I'm wrong) was converted into C code, probably using some third party utility. Than they rewrited some heavily used routines completely in x86 assembler for speed, and rewrited non-portable routines (file handling, input handling, video) to get fully running x86 executable. Compiler used to put all this together was Watcom C - sw(o)s.exe contains whole Watcom run-time library, both 16 and 32-bit versions.
```
\- @Playaveli

More info about the DOS version [here](https://sensiblesoccer.de/forum/editing-programming/4355-about-swos-programming-knowledge)

### History of `swos-port`

In the early 2000s, Zlatko Karakas and his cousin got hooked on Sensible World of Soccer (SWOS) but hit a snag: no two-player keyboard support. Fresh from learning machine code and taking a compiler course, Zlatko reverse-engineered the input routines and hacked in two-player keyboard play. Hex editing soon hit its limits, so in 2004 he created SWOS++ - a tiny loader patched into the game that brings in a separate SWOS++ binary at runtime (DLL-style). That worked well until DOS constraints capped progress, leading to `swos-port`, a cross-platform re-creation.

The workflow evolved from raw hex patches to NASM/MASM x86 assembly with advanced macros, then gradually to C, and ultimately C++ for growing systems like multiplayer. Zlatko's toolkit included IDA Pro, hex editors, NASM/MASM, Perl scripts, and piles of notes and diagrams. Exploration of SWOS formats also produced SWPE (SWOS Picture Editor). As knowledge accumulated, "static emulation" became feasible - mixing emulated chunks of the original with manually decompiled parts and new code.

Technically, swos-port starts from a full disassembly (one big .asm), converted to C++ with x86 and 68k registers modeled as variables and carefully controlled memory access to preserve original assumptions. Some code is removed or replaced, external variables are introduced, and the generated core is linked with hand-written input, graphics, and other systems. It's a long-running side project pursued in bursts (often between jobs), adding up to several years of effort. A key inspiration for making SWOS++ a proper add-on was Swedish Yankspankers' TA Demo Recorder for Total Annihilation, which showed how powerful reverse-engineered enhancements could be.

This is a **memory map** for an Amiga system showing key address ranges and how they can be used:

- **CHIP_RAM**: Main shared RAM the CPU and custom chips (Agnus/Denise/Paula) can access - for code, data, and graphics/audio buffers.
- **CIAB** and **CIAA (`0xBFE000`-`0xBFEFFF`, 4 KB, `rw`)**: The two Complex Interface Adapters - memory-mapped I/O registers for timers, keyboard/joystick, serial/parallel, etc.
- **AMIGA_CUSTOM**: Custom-chip register block (blitter, copper, bitplanes, audio, sprites, interrupts).    
- **KICK_ROM**: The Kickstart ROM with the OS core; readable/executable but not writable.

Permissions indicate whether each region is **readable (r)**, **writable (w)**, and/or **executable (x)**.

#### export_sparse_asm.py

[export_sparse_asm.py](IDAPro/Scripts/export_sparse_asm.py) is an **IDA 9-friendly "sparse assembly" exporter** that writes a clean, readable `.s` file containing just the _interesting_ heads (code/data items), labels, prototypes, and comments - without dumping every single byte. It iterates segments in address order (optionally skipping Amiga MMIO segments like `AMIGA_CUSTOM`, `CIAA`, `CIAB`), emits an `ORG 0x...` at each segment start and again only when there's a real hole of unknown bytes, and then walks heads to print one disassembly line per item with a fixed indent. For functions, it prints a labeled header, a **prototype** reconstructed from the function's `tinfo` (or a sensible fallback like `void name(...)`), and both regular and repeatable function comments. Inside functions it can also emit **intra-function code labels** (e.g., `loc_...`) and **data labels** so that cross-references stay meaningful.

A key feature is robust **comment handling** for IDA 9's wrapped/overflow comments. The script captures the base disassembly line (optionally keeping EOL comments), then collects indented/anterior and extra posterior/anterior comment blocks, and **deduplicates** any lines that merely repeat the EOL text - so you don't get the same comment echoed three times. It also pads EOL semicolons for neat formatting, and avoids `ORG` spam by detecting genuine unknown-data gaps rather than interleaved items. The result is a compact, navigable assembly listing that's ideal for code review, porting, or feeding into documentation - focused on structure (labels, prototypes, comments) rather than raw bytes.

#### sws_menu.amiga.py

[export_sparse_asm.py](IDAPro/Scripts/sws_menu.amiga.py) is an IDAPython **menu beautifier** for the Amiga build of SWOS - a faithful port of Zlatko Karakaš's [sws_menu_x86.idc](IDAPro/Scripts/sws_menu_x86.idc), adapted to the Amiga menu data layout and IDA 9.x APIs. You run it with the cursor on a menu table and it non-destructively **formats the raw menu blob into readable fields**, without renaming any symbols. It systematically converts bytes/words/dwords into proper data items, applies **offset rendering** for function pointers (`op_off`), **decimal/signed rendering** for numeric fields (`op_dec` + sign fix for negative literals), and annotates everything with clear comments so the structure is self-documenting in IDA.

The script recognizes the menu header (four dwords: init/return/draw/default entry), then walks entries until the **sentinel** `-999` (0xFB39) "end menu", handling **start menu** (`-998`), **template mode** (`-997`) and **coordinate mode switches** (`0xFFFE`\=wide, `0xFFFF`\=byte). In template or entry blocks it parses the standard x,y,width,height coordinates (byte or word based on mode), and then decodes a stream of **typed chunks**:

- `1` invisible entry; `2` navigation links (left/right/up/down); `3` custom background proc (pointer); `4` entry+frame **color flags** (pretty-printed to human color names); `5/9/21` sprite background/foreground/copy; `7/15/16/13/14` function hooks (foreground, before/after draw, on-select, input mask); `8/10/11/12/22` string/text forms (with **string flags**: color, font size, alignment; tables and multi-line pointers), and small two-byte "skip" args for `17-20`. It also prints a "control mask" explanation for input flags (fire/up/down/left/right variants). Throughout, it guards against accidental mis-signing (only toggles signed display when a negative literal is actually present), and it uses IDA's current types/comments where possible. Net effect: messy menu data becomes a **clean, browsable structure with comments and correct renderings**, tailored to Amiga's formats while preserving the original names.

#### Changes to `idaxml.py`

This patch makes IDA's Ghidra-export XML far more "Ghidra-friendly," with cleaner type strings, real register-storage metadata, and correct array/size descriptions - so your downstream Ghidra import needs less guessing and fewer fix-ups. It adds a normalization layer (`normalize_for_ghidra`) that rewrites MS/IDA type spellings into the shorter names Ghidra expects (e.g., `unsigned __int8` to `uchar`, strips `struct/union/enum/class` tags, removes calling-convention/attr tokens like `__usercall`, `__cdecl`, `__ptr64`, etc.), tidies whitespace, and preserves pointer spacing. Where available, it now prefers **actual IDA tinfo declarations** at addresses (`get_decl_from_tinfo_at`) for `<DEFINED_DATA>` so arrays and pointers (e.g., `Type *[32]`) are exported as a single, accurate declaration, and then normalizes those strings before writing them to XML.

Function export gains much richer calling-convention detail without over-asserting: it **only** marks `CALLING_CONVENTION="__usercall"` (and `CUSTOM_STORAGE`) if the IDA prototype text truly contains `__usercall`. It also lifts **register-backed parameters and returns** from IDA 9's func details and emits them as `<REGISTER_VAR>` elements and `<RETURN_TYPE>` with a concrete **register name**, including width-aware mapping on 68k data registers (`D0W`, `D0B`, etc.). If IDA says the function returns `void`, the exporter forces `<RETURN_TYPE void/>` so Ghidra won't infer a spurious D0 return. On the data/UDT side, `export_members()` is rewritten to properly handle **multi-dimensional arrays** (e.g., `byte[10][35]`) by walking nested array types, computing the true total size, and keeping the full bracket sequence in the XML. `get_member_type()` now prefers typed pointer declarations (e.g., `TeamGeneralInfo *`) and UDT names instead of generic flags, and all member/datatype strings pass through the same normalization to keep names consistent. Finally, a few new XML tokens (e.g., `PRESERVED_REGISTERS`, `REGISTER_ELEM`) are introduced for future use, and scattered writes now route through normalization - yielding exports that import cleanly into Ghidra with fewer post-processing scripts and much better fidelity for pointers, arrays, registers, and calling conventions.

You can view the full patch @ [idaxml.patch](IDAPro/idaxml.patch)

#### amiga_call_graph.py

`amiga_call_graph.py` is a Ghidra script that exports a _reachable call graph_ starting from the function currently under your cursor. It does a depth-first search over direct call sites (JSR/BSR/etc.), collecting every callee it can reach, optionally filtering out externals and thunks. The functions are then sorted by entry address and emitted to a single `StartFunctionName.c` file. The file begins with a banner and a clean list of C function prototypes synthesized from each function's return type, calling convention (if present), and parameters - so you get a quick, compilable-looking signature map of the slice of code you care about.

Optionally, it also decompiles each reached function with Ghidra's `DecompInterface` (Parameter ID enabled, "decompile" simplification) and appends the _raw_ decompiler output after the prototypes, labeling each block with the function name and entry address. Crucially, it writes the file in binary mode and preserves the decompiler's line endings verbatim to avoid mangling formatting. There's a toggle to re-run auto-analysis on the collected bodies (if your Ghidra build exposes `AutoAnalysisManager`), as well as configurable flags for including thunks/externals and a per-function decompile timeout. The save dialog lets you pick either a directory (it auto-names the file) or a specific filename (it adds `.c` if missing). In short: this script is a one-click way to harvest a coherent, address-ordered "mini-module" of prototypes plus (optionally) decompiled C for all functions reachable from a chosen entry point - perfect for staging focused refactors, code reviews, or AI-assisted cleanups.

#### amiga_prototypes.py

`amiga_prototypes.py` is a quick, one-shot exporter for **function prototypes** from your current Ghidra program. It walks every discovered function **in address order** (the binary's natural layout), formats a C-style prototype for each (return type, optional calling convention, name, and parameters), and writes them to a single **.txt** file you choose. Varargs are preserved (`...`), parameter names and types come from Ghidra's datatypes, and if anything is missing it falls back gracefully (e.g., to `int` or `param`). The result is a clean, linear list of signatures that's perfect for building headers, searching for API surfaces, or seeding decompiled modules with consistent declarations.

A couple of toggles let you trim noise: by default it **skips externals** (import stubs) and **thunks** (wrapper functions), but you can flip those flags if you want a complete picture. Under the hood it uses the FunctionManager's forward iterator to preserve address order, and a small helper normalizes type/parameter display names so the output stays readable. When it's done, it prints how many prototypes were written and where, giving you a simple, reproducible snapshot of the program's callable surface.

#### amiga_sanitize.py

`amiga_sanitize.py` is a two-pass **IDA-XML  to  Ghidra** importer that turns metadata from an IDA export into precise, compiler-like function signatures and correctly-typed MMIO data in your Amiga SWOS Ghidra project. **Pass 1 (FUNCTIONS)** reads each `<FUNCTION>` from the XML and applies an explicit `__usercall` signature with **custom register storage**: it maps every `<REGISTER_VAR>` to an actual 68k register via Ghidra's `VariableStorage`, sets the declared return type (and return register if given), carries over comments, and then **locks** the signature so later analysis won't undo it. The script also "sanitizes" types: it resolves built-ins and pointers, falls back to `unsigned int` or `void*` when a type can't be found, and avoids illegal `void` parameters. It normalizes register names (`d0.w`, `a1.l` to `d0`, `a1`) and wraps all updates in transactions for safety.

**Pass 2 (DEFINED\_DATA / MMIO)** walks `<DEFINED_DATA>` nodes to define hardware registers as **volatile** scalars at their exact addresses, attaching the label from `TYPEINFO_CMT`. It enforces Amiga-specific rules: **CIA ranges** (`BFDxxx`/`BFExxx`) are forced to **8-bit** types (e.g., `uchar`) while **Custom chip** (`DFFxxx`) keeps the XML's width (typically `ushort`). The helper carefully **reuses existing exact data** when it matches, or **surgically clears** only the necessary byte range to create the right unit - avoiding unnecessary bulldozing of larger containers. Overall, the script upgrades a raw IDA XML dump into Ghidra with realistic calling conventions, register-accurate prototypes, and correctly-typed volatile MMIO, giving you cleaner decompilation and fewer false "unknown/undefined" artifacts downstream.

## GameLoop and UpdatePlayers

[GameLoop.c](SWOS2/GameLoop.c) is the outer, per-frame orchestrator: it advances global timers/state machines and gates when real play can proceed. In this code snippet, the work is centered in `UpdateGameTimersAndCameraBreakMode()`. It increments the in-game/stoppage counters, handles penalty progression, and drives game-state transitions (kick-off, half-time, full-time, extra time, showers/results screens). It also runs the whole "camera break" pipeline (the `breakCameraMode` 0 to 7/8 ladder) that freezes play, positions the ball, triggers replays/highlights, waits for players/keeper states to settle, then re-arms the match. Along the way it primes or suppresses inputs depending on menus/substitutions and special states (e.g., `ST_KEEPER_HOLDS_BALL`). In other words, GameLoop.c is the authority on _when_ football can actually happen and _what phase_ of the match we're in.

[UpdatePlayers.c](SWOS2/UpdatePlayers.c) is the core simulation loop - the "everything happens here" routine that executes the football itself once the outer loop says go. You see it being driven from `UpdateAndApplyTeamControls()`, which interprets input for _one team per frame_ (alternating teams across frames), computes directional intent and fire/quick-fire/normal-fire edges from the button counters, applies menu/substitution gating, and then calls `UpdatePlayers(team)` to realize movement, tackles/headers, animation table switches, ball interactions, and per-sprite state updates. That same `UpdatePlayers(...)` can also be hit from inside `UpdateGameTimersAndCameraBreakMode()` during panic/recovery paths (e.g., after a break sequence) to keep the simulation coherent. Practically, this means **GameLoop.c controls the cadence and high-level state of the match**, while **UpdatePlayers.c performs the per-frame physics/AI/control application**. They're tightly coupled: `UpdateGameTimersAndCameraBreakMode()` is invoked first to ensure the world is in a legal state, and `UpdateAndApplyTeamControls()` (which calls `UpdatePlayers` twice per frame across the two teams) applies the inputs and updates the on-pitch actors. This layering is why both files are pivotal: one keeps the match rules, timers, and presentation consistent; the other actually plays the football.

### What is SWOS.Slave?

`SWOS.Slave` is a **WHDLoad slave** is a tiny loader/patcher that makes an original game run cleanly from hard drive under WHDLoad (instead of from floppies). In practice, the slave:

- **Loads and relocates the game binary** (e.g., `SWOS2` plus its relocation table), placing code/data into the configured ExpMem/ChipMem.
- **Applies patches at startup** (via a patch list) to fix compatibility/snoop issues, skip copy-protection, adjust blitter/timing, and route file I/O.
- **Bridges file access** (save/load) to WHDLoad's "resload" API so saves go to a folder (e.g., `SAVE/`) instead of disks.
- **Handles WHDLoad tooltypes** like `PRELOAD`, `NOCACHE`, `NOVBRMOVE`, etc., and cooperates with options like `whdload_quit`.
- **Installs small hooks** (e.g., keyboard exit) and cleanup paths, then jumps into the game's entry point.

### SWOS vs SWOS2

The original **Sensible World of Soccer** Amiga release ships with two main game binaries:

- **SWOS** - the original executable, used on older configurations (for example, machines with Kickstart versions and CPUs below the A1200-style Kick 3.1 + 68020 setup).
- **SWOS2** - the A1200-oriented executable, tuned for later machines and used when the SSBOOT loader detects a suitable configuration.

All of the work described here focuses on **SWOS2**, which is the A1200-targeted version of the game.

#### SWOS2.REL

`SWOS2.REL` is a **separate relocation table** used by the original game's loader in conjunction with the flat, pre-relocated **SWOS2** executable image. It does **not** contain code or data itself; instead, it encodes the offsets within the SWOS2 image that must be adjusted when the image is placed in memory.

At runtime, the loader:

1. Loads the static SWOS2 binary into memory at some chosen base address.
2. Reads `SWOS2.REL` and walks its relocation entries.
3. For each relocation entry, it:
   - Interprets the value as an offset into the SWOS2 image.
   - Locates the word or long at that offset.
   - Adds the final load base to that word/long to make it a valid runtime address.

Because `SWOS2.REL` enumerates all locations in the SWOS2 image that are treated as pointers, it effectively encodes **where all absolute address references live**. That makes it an extremely valuable source of information when reverse engineering and when reconstructing a fully relocatable hunk-based build later.

#### Structure of `SWOS2.REL`

`SWOS2.REL` is a **flat array of 32-bit big-endian offsets**. There is no header, no counts, and no extra metadata - just `N` longwords, each describing where a relocatable pointer lives in the original SWOS2 image.

For example, the start of the file looks like this:

```hex
00 00 00 03  00 00 00 C2  00 00 00 C3  00 00 00 C7
00 00 00 D9  00 00 00 DF  00 00 00 E9  00 00 01 0D
...
```

Interpreted as big-endian 32-bit integers, this gives a sequence of offsets:

```text
index  raw bytes       offset (big-endian)
-----  --------------  -------------------
0      00 00 00 03     0x00000003
1      00 00 00 C2     0x000000C2
2      00 00 00 C3     0x000000C3
3      00 00 00 C7     0x000000C7
4      00 00 00 D9     0x000000D9
5      00 00 00 DF     0x000000DF
6      00 00 00 E9     0x000000E9
7      00 00 01 0D     0x0000010D
...
```

Given a known **program base** (in your IDA setup, `PROGRAM_BASE = 0x00100000`), each relocation entry is applied by:

1. Computing the effective `a0` after the game's relocation add:
```text
a0_after_add = PROGRAM_BASE + offset
```
2. Backing up one byte (because the 68k code does `tst.b -(a0)` before reading the long):
```text
ptr_ea = a0_after_add - 1
```
3. Reading the 32-bit value at `ptr_ea`, which is the **relocatable pointer value**.
4. Treating that value as the pre-relocation target address inside the SWOS image.

For example, for the very first entry:

- Offset bytes: `00 00 00 03` → `offset = 0x00000003`
- `a0_after_add = 0x00100000 + 0x00000003 = 0x00100003`
- `ptr_ea = 0x00100003 - 1 = 0x00100002`
- The long at `0x00100002` is `0x001000C4`, so the target is `start` at `0x001000C4`.

This matches the first line of the relocation dump:

```text
0000: off=0x00000003 ptr_ea=0x00100002 val=0x001000C4 -> target=0x001000C4 [C] start  jmp     start
```

Likewise, later entries map cleanly to other code and data symbols (interrupt handlers, globals, drive string tables, etc.), e.g.:

```text
0015: off=0x00000233 ptr_ea=0x00100232 val=0x00100268 -> target=0x00100268 [D] kDriveListPtrs  lea (kDriveListPtrs).l,a3
0016: off=0x00000269 ptr_ea=0x00100268 val=0x00100278 -> target=0x00100278 [D] aDf0            dc.l aDf0
...
```

This simple **"array of big-endian offsets from the program base"** structure is what makes `SWOS2.REL` such a rich source of information: by replaying the relocation logic against the IDA database, we can reconstruct exactly which words in the original static image were treated as addresses, and where they pointed.

### `export_sparse_asm.py`

`export_sparse_asm.py` is an **IDAPython script for IDA 9.0** that runs on the SWOS2 database which matches the original static executable layout (1:1 bytes). It is specifically designed to consume the original `SWOS2.REL` file and use IDA's analysis to generate a relocation table text file.

It performs two key tasks:

1. **Reads and parses `SWOS2.REL` directly from disk**  
The script opens the original `SWOS2.REL`, walks the relocation stream, and reconstructs the list of relocation entries (i.e. "these offsets in the original image contain relocatable addresses"). Each entry is treated as a big-endian 32-bit offset from the program base, matching the way the original game and WHDLoad slave apply relocations.

2. **Uses the IDA 9.0 API to correlate relocations with the loaded database and display its references in the disassembly**
Using the IDA 9.x API the script maps each relocation entry to an effective address (EA) in the IDA database and inspects the surrounding code/data and types. From this it generates a relocation dump (`SWOS2_reloc_dump.txt`) summarising the relocation entries in a readable, EA-based form.

### SWOS2 Amiga Hunk executable

The next step is to take the sparse assembly produced by `export_sparse_asm.py`, tidy and structure it (adding meaningful labels, types, comments, and segment boundaries), and then **rebuild SWOS2 as a true Amiga hunk executable**.

In this new build:

- Code and data are placed into proper **HUNK_CODE** and **HUNK_DATA** segments.
- The assembler/linker generate **relocation hunks** instead of relying on an external flat relocation file.
- Absolute addresses are replaced by **labels and relocatable expressions**, which the linker can freely move.

Moving to a hunk-based SWOS2 gives several key benefits:

- **Relocation flexibility** - the code and data no longer have to live at exactly the same physical addresses as the original static build. The OS can load the program where it wants, and the relocation hunks will patch everything automatically.
- **Room for growth** - new code and data can be added (e.g. new gameplay logic, graphics structures, tables) without constantly fighting fixed addresses or overflowing the original layout.
- **Better toolchain integration** - once the game is a standard hunk executable, it can be linked with additional object files, libraries, and even mixed-language modules, just like any other Amiga program.

### Floppy to Hard Disk Drive

In the original setup, the static SWOS2 image is launched via **WHDLoad** with a `SWOS.Slave` file. That slave injects callbacks to handle disk access and decompression by calling WHDLoad's `resload_*` entry points (for example, for getting file sizes, loading files, optionally decrunching data, and saving/deleting files). From the game's point of view, many of these operations still assume floppy-style paths like `DFx:`.

In the new SWOS2 hunk-based build, the goal is to:

1. **Move file access from floppy-style devices to hard-disk-style devices**, e.g. from `DF0:` to `DH0:` (or other system volumes), so that SWOS2 behaves like a normal hard-disk-installed game.
2. **Eliminate the dependency on WHDLoad's `resload_*` functions** by implementing our own file I/O stubs directly inside the SWOS2 hunk executable, written in 68k assembly and linked as part of the program.
3. **Bind all file operations directly to AmigaDOS or equivalent system services**, so launching the game is just running the SWOS2 hunk executable, without going through WHDLoad at all.

Once all call sites that previously relied on `resload_GetFileSize`, `resload_LoadFile`, `resload_LoadFileDecrunch`, `resload_DeleteFile`, and `resload_SaveFile` have been redirected to in-executable routines, the `SWOS.Slave` file and WHDLoad are no longer required for normal gameplay. SWOS2 becomes a **fully standalone Amiga hunk executable** ("jailbroken").

At that point, development and debugging get significantly easier:

- The [Amiga Assembly](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=prb28.amiga-assembly) can be used to assemble the SWOS2 source and attach its debugger directly to the running hunk executable.
- Breakpoints, single-stepping, and inspection of registers/memory can be done directly against the real game binary, without WHDLoad's wrapper in the way.

### C Port

A clean, symbolised hunk-based SWOS2 executable also lays the groundwork for an incremental **SWOS-to-C port**.

With a proper hunk build and a modern toolchain, we can:

- Port one assembly subroutine at a time to C (or C++), link it into the same executable, and verify its behaviour against the original implementation.
- Keep the rest of the game in 68k assembly while gradually replacing pieces with higher-level code.
- Use VSCode's tooling, including the [Amiga C/C++ Compile, Debug & Profile](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=BartmanAbyss.amiga-debug) extension, which ships with **vasm** (the same assembler used in the Amiga Assembly extension) and a complete C/C++ toolchain, to build, debug, and profile mixed C/assembly builds.

This staged approach means we don't need a "big bang" rewrite. Instead, the C port can be evolved incrementally, with each converted routine tested in the real game environment.

The hunk-based SWOS2 executable is also the platform on which the **SWOS 25/26 Amiga version** will be built.

Planned goals for this future version include:

Because the new SWOS2 hunk build removes the rigid address dependencies and external WHDLoad file handling, all of these changes can be implemented in a more maintainable, modular way. # Debugging without a debugger

When launching SWOS2 under **WHDLoad**, you cannot attach the Amiga Assembly VSCode extension's debugger directly to the running game. Instead, you rely on low-level techniques that let you *observe* control flow and state by manipulating hardware registers and deliberately triggering exceptions.

This section describes two practical techniques:

- Using the **COLOR00** register to visualise execution paths.
- Using **illegal / NOP opcodes** to trigger WHDLoad's core dump mechanism and then analysing the dumps with tools like **HxD** and the assembler **.lst** listing.

---

## 1. Using COLOR00 to trace execution

The Amiga's first colour register, `COLOR00`, controls the background colour. By writing different values to this register at key points in the code, you can tell *where* the CPU is executing just by watching the screen.

Example (set background to bright red):

```asm
move.w  #$F00,(COLOR00).l   ; Red
```

![](/images/debug_00.png)

Some useful 12-bit RGB examples (OCS/ECS format: `0xRGB`, 4 bits per channel):

```asm
move.w  #$000,(COLOR00).l   ; Black
move.w  #$F00,(COLOR00).l   ; Red
move.w  #$0F0,(COLOR00).l   ; Green
move.w  #$00F,(COLOR00).l   ; Blue
move.w  #$FF0,(COLOR00).l   ; Yellow
move.w  #$FFF,(COLOR00).l   ; White
```

Typical usage patterns:

- **Entry/exit markers** - Set `COLOR00` to one colour on function entry and another on exit to see if/when a routine runs.
- **Branch tracing** - Use different colours on each side of a conditional branch to see which path is taken.
- **Critical sections** - Mark "should never happen" code paths with a loud colour (e.g. bright red) to make failures visually obvious.

Because `COLOR00` is a simple hardware write, it is a very low-overhead way to gain insight into control flow when no debugger is attached.

---

## 2. Using illegal and NOP opcodes with WHDLoad core dumps

When running under WHDLoad, an **illegal instruction** will cause WHDLoad to interrupt the game and show an error dialog with the current PC and other state. You can leverage this behavior to capture full memory/register dumps at interesting points.

### 2.1. ILLEGAL vs NOP

On 68000:

- `ILLEGAL` is encoded as **`$4AFC`**.
- `NOP` is encoded as **`$4E71`**.

A common pattern is:

- Replace an existing instruction with `ILLEGAL` (`$4AFC`) to *trap* execution when it reaches that point.
- If you need to keep instruction count/size stable (for the **static version** with hard-coded offsets), use `NOP` (`$4E71`) to pad out or neutralise instructions without changing the byte count.

> **Important (static 1:1 version):**  
> When patching the original static image you **must** keep the total byte count identical. Shifting code or data will break all hard-coded offsets used with the original `SWOS2.REL`. That means any injected ILLEGAL/NOP sequence must be the same size as the code it replaces.

### 2.2. Triggering the WHDLoad error dialog

Once you've patched in an ILLEGAL instruction, run the game under WHDLoad. When execution hits that opcode, WHDLoad will display a message similar to:

> `Exception "Illegal Instruction" ($10) at $8760EC (ExpMem $800EC) occurred.`

![](/images/debug_01.png)

#### Other WHDLoad-trapped errors (at a glance)

Besides illegal instruction traps, WHDLoad intercepts a lot of other problems and turns them into readable error dialogs. This effectively gives you "poor-man’s debugging" information: a description, a PC, sometimes a memory range, and often the name of the `resload_` function involved.

Typical categories you’ll see include:

- **DOS / file I/O errors** - read/write/scan/delete failures on specific files.
- **CPU exceptions** - address/bus/illegal instruction, always with a PC.
- **OS emulation / `resload_` API errors** - bad SR/SP, destroyed registers, invalid `PLCMD_*` patch commands, failed decrunch/delta/relocate.
- **Kickstart / data integrity issues** - invalid Kickstart images, corrupt relocation/patch tables, CRC mismatches.
- **Hardware misuse** - blitter not waited for, blitter out of bounds, copperlist problems, incomplete MMU trees.
- **Self-modifying code / SMC checks** - modified opcodes detected, unsupported addressing modes for Snoop/S.
- **CPU / chipset / video mode requirements** - needs 68020+, AGA, PAL/NTSC, etc.
- **Stack / interrupts / VBR / CACR problems** - bad SP or modified VBR/CACR on entering `resload_*`.
- **Misc config issues** - XPK not cached, PreLoad/Examine errors, invalid QuitKey/controller combinations.

When you hit one of these dialogs, treat it like a mini crash report: note the **PC**, any mentioned **address or range**, and the **error type**. You can then cross-reference that information with your `.lst` file and disassembly, and-in combination with the WHDLoad dump files-narrow down where your code or data is going wrong even without a "real" debugger attached.

![](/images/debug_02.png)

From this dialog:

1. Click **"Make CoreDump"**.
2. WHDLoad will write a set of dump files into `DH0:C` (or the configured WHDLoad directory):

   - `*.whdl_dump`
   - `*.whdl_expmem`
   - `*.whdl_memory`
   - `*.whdl_register`

### 2.3. What the WHDLoad dump files contain

The exact format is internal to WHDLoad, but for debugging SWOS2 you can treat them roughly as:

- **`.whdl_register`** - A **text file** with a snapshot of all CPU registers (D0-D7, A0-A7, SR, PC, etc.) plus some WHDLoad state. This is your starting point for understanding what the CPU was doing when the ILLEGAL occurred.
- **`.whdl_memory`** - A **binary dump of main memory** (chip/fast) as seen by the program at the time of the exception. Addresses like `$0010xxxx` can usually be located directly in this file.
- **`.whdl_expmem`** - A **binary dump of the expansion memory area** used by WHDLoad (`ExpMem`). If the error message mentions `ExpMem $800EC`, for example, you can subtract the expansion base (e.g. `$80000`) to get an offset inside this file.
- **`.whdl_dump`** - A WHDLoad-specific consolidated dump intended mainly for WHDLoad authors; you typically don't need to touch this directly for day-to-day SWOS2 work.

### 2.4. Inspecting dumps with HxD

[HxD](https://mh-nexus.de/en/hxd/) is a versatile hex editor that you can use to inspect the `.whdl_memory` and `.whdl_expmem` binaries:

1. Open `*.whdl_memory` or `*.whdl_expmem` in HxD.
2. Use **Search → Goto...** (or Ctrl+G) and select "hexadecimal offset".
3. To locate an address reported by WHDLoad:

   - If the exception shows `PC = $0010ABCD`, you can usually use `$0010ABCD` directly as an offset in `.whdl_memory` (or subtract the base if the dump is offset).
   - If the exception shows `ExpMem $800EC`, subtract the expansion base (e.g. `$80000`) to get the offset (`$800EC - $80000 = $EC`) and jump to that offset in `.whdl_expmem`.

This lets you see exactly what bytes were at the faulting address and around it at the moment of the crash.

![](/images/debug_03.png)

---

## 3. Using the vasm listing (`.lst`) with `.whdl_register`

When building the static version, run `vasm` with a listing option, for example:

```bash
vasmm68k_mot ... -L build/SWOS2.lst ...
```

This generates a **listing file** (`SWOS2.lst`) that interleaves:

- Source lines
- Final addresses
- Assembled opcodes

Here's a small section from the `SWOS2.lst` file:
```

                            	 19260: ;      A6 -> right team in-game struct
                            	 19261: GameLoop:
01:0010E8D6 42790012F6FC    	 19262:                 clr.w   (gameCanceled).l
01:0010E8DC 42790010F056    	 19263:                 clr.w   (instantReplayFlag).l

01:0010E8F4 323C00A8        	 19267:                 move.w  #168,d1

01:0010E902 661A            	 19270:                 bne.s   pre_frame_init
```

This is invaluable when combined with WHDLoad's register snapshot:

1. Open `*.whdl_register` in a text editor.
2. Note key values, especially:

   - **PC** - the program counter at the time of the ILLEGAL.
   - **SR** - the status register (condition codes, interrupt level).
   - Any registers that look relevant (e.g. A0/A1 for pointers, D0/D1 for loop counters).

3. Determine whether the PC is in main memory or expansion memory:

   - If it looks like a normal code address (e.g. `$0010xxxx`), treat it as a main memory address.
   - If it matches an `ExpMem` range, adjust by the expansion base (as you did when using HxD).

4. In `SWOS2.lst`, search for the **hex address** of the PC.  
   The listing will show you:

   - The exact instruction that triggered the ILLEGAL.
   - The surrounding instructions and labels (function name, local labels, etc.).
   - The assembled bytes, which you can cross-check against `.whdl_memory` or `.whdl_expmem`.

By combining:

- The **PC and register state** from `.whdl_register`,
- The **raw bytes** from `.whdl_memory` / `.whdl_expmem` via HxD, and
- The **symbolic listing** from `SWOS2.lst`,

you can reconstruct what the engine was doing at the moment of failure and track down bugs even without an interactive debugger.

---

## 4. Why we eventually remove the WHDLoad dependency

These techniques are essential while we're still running via WHDLoad and the static version, because we can't attach the Amiga Assembly VSCode debugger directly to the game process.

One of the long-term goals of converting SWOS2 into a **stand-alone Amiga Hunk executable** (with its own HDD file I/O routines instead of WHDLoad's `resload_*` helpers) is to **eliminate the WHDLoad layer** entirely. Once SWOS2 can be launched as a normal Hunk executable:

- We can run it under the Amiga Assembly VSCode extension's debugger,
- Set breakpoints and single-step directly in our source code,
- And make development and porting (e.g. to C) much easier.

Those debugger-based workflows are covered in the following sections once the custom HDD routines and stand-alone Hunk build are in place.

## 5. Cooperating with AmigaDOS: temporarily yielding the level 2 interrupt

Once SWOS2 stopped using WHDLoad's `resload_*` helpers and started calling `dos.library` directly, a new class of problems appeared: **illegal instructions and Gurus inside `dos_Open` / `dos_Read`**.

The underlying reason is:

- The game **replaces the OS level-2 autovector** with its own keyboard interrupt (`Int2KeyboardHandler`).
- `dos.library` itself relies on **Exec's own level-2 handler** (and uses privileged instructions like `ORI #$2000,SR`) while doing I/O.
- If we call into DOS while our custom handler is still installed, the OS ends up running code that assumes a different interrupt setup than what we actually have, which can lead to illegal instructions or stack corruption.

The safest fix is to:

> **Temporarily give level-2 back to Exec/DOS for the duration of each disk I/O call, then restore the game's handler afterwards.**

We already saved the original vector at startup:

```asm
        ; Save original Exec/OS autovectors
        move.l  LEVEL_1_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0),S_SavedInt1
        move.l  LEVEL_2_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0),S_SavedInt2
        move.l  LEVEL_3_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0),S_SavedInt3
        move.l  LEVEL_4_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0),S_SavedInt4
        move.l  LEVEL_5_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0),S_SavedInt5
```

So the WHDLoad compatibility stubs in `resload.s` do this dance around every call that touches `dos.library`.

For example, the `_LoadFile` wrapper that Rob Northen's loader calls:

```asm
; --- _LoadFile ------------------------------------------------------------
; In:  A0 = filename, A1 = destination buffer
; Out: global 'size' updated with length; caller registers restored
_LoadFile:
        movem.l d0-d1/a0-a2,-(sp)

        move.l  a0,a2                  ; save filename

        ; Exec owns level 2 while we do DOS I/O
        move.l  S_VBR(pc),a0
        move.l  S_SavedInt2,LEVEL_2_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0)

        move.l  a2,a0                  ; restore filename for resload_LoadFile
        jsr     resload_LoadFile       ; D0 = length, D1 = error

        move.l  S_VBR(pc),a0
        move.l  #Int2KeyboardHandler,LEVEL_2_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0)

        ; store returned length for rob_*
        lea     size(pc),a0
        move.l  d0,(a0)

        movem.l (sp)+,d0-d1/a0-a2
        rts
```

The same pattern is used for the other WHDLoad-style entry points:

- `_GetFileSize` → `resload_GetFileSize`
- `_SaveFile`    → `resload_SaveFile`
- `_Deletefile`  → `resload_Deletefile`
- `_ListFiles`   → `resload_ListFiles`

Each of these:

1. Saves the game's registers (via `movem.l`).
2. Writes `oldInt2` back into `LEVEL_2_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR` to restore the original DOS/Exec handler.
3. Calls the new `resload_*` implementation, which internally uses `dos_Open`, `dos_Read`, `dos_Write`, etc.
4. Re-installs `Int2KeyboardHandler` as the level-2 autovector.
5. Restores registers and returns to the Rob Northen loader / game code.

This keeps the **visible behaviour of all existing `resload_*` call sites identical** (same prototypes, same `size` global), while avoiding illegal instructions inside the DOS I/O path.

## 6. Cleanly returning from SWOS2 back to DOS

Once SWOS2 runs as a normal Hunk executable with AmigaDOS file I/O, we also need a **clean way to exit back to the shell / Workbench** instead of just "falling off the end" or leaving interrupts and DMA enabled.

Some of this is covered in the [Amiga 500: Bare-Metal Startup Code](https://bumbershootsoft.wordpress.com/2024/08/10/amiga-500-bare-metal-startup-code/) blog post.

There are three pieces to this:

### 6.1. Mapping a key to "quit to DOS"

The keyboard hook (`KBHook`) is installed as part of the custom level-2 handler. It already sees raw keycodes via CIA:

```asm
        xdef    KBHook
KBHook
    move.b  $bfec01,d0
    move.w  d0,-(a7)
    not.b   d0
    ror.b   #1,d0
    cmp.b   _keyexit(pc),d0
    beq.b   quit
    move.w  (a7)+,d0
    rts

quit:
    move.w  (a7)+,d0
    move.w  #1,g_quitToDos
    rts

_keyexit	dc.b	$46		;ws_keyexit = Del
        xdef    g_quitToDos
g_quitToDos:
        dc.w    0
```

Instead of trying to tear everything down directly inside the interrupt handler (which risks stack mismatches and re-entrancy issues), the project uses a **global flag** (e.g. `g_quitToDos`) and checks it in the main loops.

A typical pattern in a polling loop looks like:

```asm
    tst.w   g_quitToDos
    bne.s   intro_continue  ; or branch to a clean exit path
```

This lets the game finish its inner loop, unwind to a safe point (usually `main`), and then call the final cleanup routine.

### 6.2. Restoring interrupts and hardware state: `ExitToDos`

At the very top level, after `main` returns, the entry point simply calls a dedicated cleanup routine:

```asm
start:
    ...
    jsr     main
    jsr     ExitToDos
    rts
```

`ExitToDos` is responsible for putting the machine back into a state that AmigaDOS expects:

```asm
        xdef    ExitToDos
ExitToDos:

        move.l  S_VBR(pc),a0

        move.l  S_SavedInt1,LEVEL_1_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0)
        move.l  S_SavedInt2,LEVEL_2_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0)
        move.l  S_SavedInt3,LEVEL_3_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0)
        move.l  S_SavedInt4,LEVEL_4_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0)
        move.l  S_SavedInt5,LEVEL_5_INTERRUPT_AUTOVECTOR(a0)

       ; Wait for blitter idle again (paranoia)
        btst    #14-8,(DMACONR).l
.blt_idle_exit:
        btst    #14-8,(DMACONR).l
        bne.s   .blt_idle_exit

        ; Now safe to kill DMA and interrupts
        ;move.w  #$01FF,(DMACON).l     ; Disable all DMA channels
        ;move.w  #$3FFF,(INTENA).l     ; Disable all interrupts

        ; Restore original view via graphics.library
        move.l  S_GfxBase(pc),a6         ; Load gfxbase
        move.l  gfx_copinit(a6),COP1LC   ; Restore coplist pointer 1
        move.l  gfx_LOFlist(a6),COP2LC   ; Restore coplist pointer 2
        clr.w   COPJMP1                  ; Make Copper use restored pointer
        
        ; Restore DMA / interrupts / ADKCON
        move.w  S_SavedDmaCon,(DMACON).l
        move.w  S_SavedIntEna,(INTENA).l
        move.w  S_SavedAdkCon,(ADKCON).l

        move.l  S_SavedView,a1
        beq.s   .no_view                 ; (paranoia)
        jsr     GfxLoadView(a6)
        move.l  S_GfxBase(pc),a6
        jsr     GfxWaitTOF(a6)
        jsr     GfxWaitTOF(a6)

.no_view:

        tst.w   S_FromWB
        beq.s   .done

        ; --- Hand control back to Workbench / CLI ---
        move.l  4.w,a6                  ; Exec base

        tst.l   S_WBMsg
        beq.s   .no_wbmsg
        move.l  S_WBMsg(pc),a1
        jsr     ExecReplyMsg(a6)
.no_wbmsg:

        ; Close graphics.library if we opened it
        move.l  S_GfxBase(pc),a1
        beq.s   .done
        jsr     ExecCloseLib(a6)

.done:

        movea.l S_SavedSP,sp
        moveq   #0,d0
        rts
```

Key points:

- **All** hardware vectors we touched (levels 1-5) are restored from the saved `oldIntX` values taken at startup.
- CIAs and custom-chip interrupts are disabled so DOS doesn't inherit stray interrupt sources.
- DMA is turned off and the background colour is reset, so the user is dropped back to a clean shell / Workbench screen.

Because the program was launched as a regular AmigaOS process (from Shell or via a script), a simple `RTS` from `start` is enough to return control to DOS. There's no need to call `dos_Exit()` explicitly (and in practice, doing so after heavy custom interrupt work can hang under some environments).

### 6.3. Optional: quitting the emulator from a script

If running under UAE / FS-UAE, a tiny `SWOS` script in the same directory can wrap the executable and then immediately request that the emulator shuts down once the game returns:

```amiga
CD SYS:SWOS
data/SWOS2
```

From the game's perspective, it just exits back to DOS via `ExitToDos` and returns from `start`. From the user's perspective, double-clicking the icon:

- launches SWOS2,
- the game runs in full-screen as a stand-alone executable,
- and when they hit **Del** (or otherwise exit the game), control returns to the script, which calls `UAEquit` and closes the emulator.

Taken together, the **interrupt hand-off around `resload_*`** and the **clean shutdown path in `ExitToDos`** complete the journey from "WHDLoad-only slave" to a proper **stand-alone Amiga Hunk executable** that plays nicely with both AmigaDOS and modern debugging tools.

### 7. Amiga Assembly Debugger

![](/images/debug_04.png)

Now that SWOS2 runs as a **stand-alone Hunk executable** with normal AmigaDOS I/O, we can finally bring the Amiga Assembly VSCode debugger into the loop instead of flying blind through hex dumps and printf-style hacks. The game can be launched directly under the debugger (or via a script that the debugger controls), which means all of your assembled source files line up with the running code: you can set **source-level breakpoints** in `SWOS2.s` / `resload.s`, single-step through instructions, and immediately see the effect on registers and memory. Instead of guessing why `UnpackMenu` jumped into space or why `LoaderIntroWaitForFireOrTimeout` blew its stack, you can just stop inside those routines, inspect `A0/A1/D0/D1`, and watch each write to `g_currentMenu` or `currentGameTick` as it happens.

On top of that, the debugger gives you “modern IDE” style features mapped onto the Amiga: **watch expressions** for key globals (e.g. `g_quitToDos`, `g_currentMenuPtr`, `size`), **memory views** of chip/fast RAM to track graphics and buffers, and **step-into/step-out** control around your new `resload_*` implementations and Rob Northen loader stubs. You can set breakpoints on your custom interrupts (`Int2KeyboardHandler`, `Int3TimerHandler`) to see exactly when CIA events fire, or break on the return from a `dos_Read`/`dos_Open` wrapper to confirm file sizes and destinations. In practice, this turns SWOS2 from a black box that occasionally Guru-meditates into a **fully inspectable process**, making reverse-engineering, refactoring, and the eventual C port vastly more manageable.

Be sure to visit the [Visual Studio Code Amiga Assembly Wiki](https://github.com/prb28/vscode-amiga-assembly/wiki) for more details on how to use the debugging features.

# CPC Mastering tools

These are some tools to make CDT and DSK files to use with Amstrad CPC
emulators.

There's also a BASIC loader that will display a loading screen and
load a program.

Both CDT and DSK will have 4 files:

 1. loader.bas: sets the palette, loads the screen and loads the game
 2. loading: the loading screen data in SCR format (160x200 pixels, mode 0)
 3. pal: the loading screen palette (16 colours, mode 0)
 3. game: the program to run

## Requirements

 - cmake
 - gcc
 - make
 - python and pillow
 - a POSIX environment, likely

In a Debian based distro:

	sudo apt-get install build-essential cmake python-pillow

And that should do it!

Run `make` to build the tools.

## Making a CDT (tape)

Create the base CDT (change "MYGAME" to whatever you want):

    2cdt -s 0 -n -r MYGAME loader.bas master.cdt

Notes:

 - 2cdt always shows the help EVEN IF IT WORKS FINE
 - You'll need to run this always first to "blank" the tape
 - I recommend using `-s 0` because the default `-s 1` is a bit too fast
   if you really plan to load the game from cassette on a real 464 that
   is 30+ years old!

Add to the base CDT the palette file (see below how to generate one):

    2cdt -s 0 -F 2 -L 0xa000 -r PAL pal master.cdt

Add the SCR:

    2cdt -s 0 -F 2 -L 0xc000 -r LOADING loading master.cdt

Finally add your program:

    2cdt -s 0 -r GAME -X EXEC -L LOAD prog.bin master.cdt

Where:

 - EXEC is the execution address in hex (eg. 0x401b)
 - LOAD is the loading address (eg. 0x4000)

## Making a DSK (disc)

Create an empty disc:

    idsk master.dsk -n

Add the loader:

    idsk master.dsk -i loader.bas

Note: you can copy `loader.bas` to `disc.bas` and import that filename.

Add the palette (seel belo how to generate one):

    idsk master.dsk -i pal -t 1 -c a000

Add the loading screen:

    idsk master.dsk -i loading -t 1 -c c000

Add the game:

    idsk master.dsk -i game -t 1 -e EXEC -c LOAD

Where:

 - EXEC is the execution address in hex (eg. 401b)
 - LOAD is the loading address (eg. 4000)

## Preparing the SCR file

Create a SCR from an indexed PNG file:

    png2crtc loading.png loading 7 0

Dump the palette:

    dump-pal.py loading.png pal

Look at the PNG sample in `example`, but the basic
requirements are:

 - Must be 160x200 pixels
 - Indexed (palette) with 16 colours from the CPC palette

The tools check that the right colours are used. You can see
`dump-pal.py` for the expected RGB values of the CPC palette.

## License

All the tools are free software and come with their own license and/or
conditions.

The tools included here for your convenience can also be found online:

2CDT
====

(c) Kevin Thacker

(Original code written in May 2000, fixed and released in May 2001)

2CDT is a utility to transfer files into a ".CDT" Tape-Image.

A ".CDT" is a tape-image file which describes the data stored on a cassette tape.
 
This file format is very powerful and can describe fast and custom loaders as well
as standard operating system formats.

The ".CDT" file format is identical to the ".TZX" format. The extension is used
to differentiate between Spectrum and Amstrad Tape-Images.

The ".TZX" file format was originally designed to store Spectrum tape programs,
it's format can be found from various sources, one of these is "World Of Spectrum":
http://www.void.jump.org/

There are a number of tools which already create .TZX files, Taper, Voc2TZX and MakeTZX.
However, these are designed to recognise Spectrum tape loaders, and so do not do well
at creating a tape-image for Amstrad formats.

This tool has been designed as a starting point for furthur Amstrad CDT tools,
and as a program to generate reference tape-images which can be used by emulator
authors to support this tape-image format in their programs.

This tool is designed to "inject" one or more file into a ".CDT" in the format written 
by the Amstrad operating system. The tool allows the user to define the ".CDT" "recording" 
method and baud rate.

2CDT	[parameters]	<source file> <output CDT filename>

parameters:
	-n		
			- Blank CDT file before use

			Use this to create a new CDT, otherwise file
			will be added to the end of an existing CDT.

	-s <speed write>
			- Write data with 'speed write' 0 or 1.

			This is the same as typing "SPEED WRITE 0" or "SPEED WRITE 1"
			in BASIC. Speed Write '0' is 1000 baud. Speed write '1' is
			2000 baud.

	-b <baud rate>  
			- Specify Baud Rate.
			
			Allows you to specify faster or slower loading.
			
	-t <method>	
			- Method to write data into TZX (for Amstrad blocks)
			0 = Pure Data Block
			1 = Turbo Loading Data Block (default)

	-m <method>
			- Method to write CPC data 
			0 = blocks (default)
			1 = headerless (Firmware function CAS READ for reading, CAS WRITE for writing )
				To be loaded with firmware function CAS READ.
				Not readable from BASIC. Allows entire program
				to be stored as a single continuous block.
			2 = Spectrum ROM loader

	-r <tape filename>
			- Give the tape file a name. Up to 16 characters.

			 This allows you to give the file on tape a different
			name to the name given on your local filesystem.

			If no name is defined, the file will be unnamed.
			This option applies to CPC 'blocks' methods only.

	-X <address>
			Define execution address (where file doesn't have header), or 
			override execution address (where file has a header)
			
	-L <address>
			Define load address (where file doesn't have header), or 
			override load address (where file has a header)

	-T <address>
			Define type (where file doesn't have header), or 
			override type address (where file has a header)
			0 = BASIC, 2 = BINARY
			
	-p <number>
			Set initial pause (default 3000ms)
	
	-P
			Add a small initial pause block for buggy emulators (e.g. old versions of Arnold)
			Not recommended. Please use newer version of this emulator.
								
Examples:

The following in a bacth file will create the master tape for 'Stranded':

REM create new CDT and put binary loader
2cdt -n -r stranded strandlod.bin stranded.cdt
REM add screen to existing CDT data
2cdt -r screen loading.bin stranded.cdt
REM add code to existing CDT data
2cdt -r code stranded.bin stranded.cdt

If you wanted to create a master tape for a game called 'Columns':

REM create new CDT and put binary loader
2cdt -n -r loader colload.bin columns.cdt
REM put binary file as headerless
2cdt -m 1 colcode.bin columns.cdt

# EXMON II

(C) 1990 Beebug

An updated version of EXMON II, with updates and code comments from
https://github.com/mincebert and https://github.com/tom-seddon. Based
on BBC Micro EXMON II version 2.02.

Additional features:

- doesn't print `EXMON II` when you press BREAK

- now includes a properly Electron-compatible version

More to come. Watch this space!

# Instructions

See `EXMONIImanual.pdf` in the repo.

# Electron-specific instructions

The manual refers to an Electron version of EXMON II, but there don't
seem to be any copies available. Perhaps it was planned, then never
released; perhaps it's simply been lost to time.

The manual's Electron notes do largely apply to this version. Please
also note the following:

- the ROM reports itself as `EXMON IIe` rather than `EXMON II`

- when using the editor, press FUNC+SHIFT+up/down to scroll to the
  next half page
  
- use `;` to toggle between hex view and disassembly

- the dual screen commands have been removed - but much of the code
  remains, so problems are possible...

# Building

## Prerequisites

### Windows

- Python 3.x

Additional dependencies are provided as pre-built EXEs in the repo.

### POSIX-type

- GNU Make (`make`)
- Python 3.x (`/usr/bin/python3`)
- [64tass](https://sourceforge.net/projects/tass64/) (`64tass`) -
  version 2974 works

## Clone the repo

The repo has submodules. Clone it with `--recursive`:

    git clone --recursive https://github.com/tom-seddon/exmon2_disassembly
	
Alternatively, if you already cloned it non-recursively, you can do
the following from inside the working copy:

    git submodule init
	git submodule update

## Build the code

Run `make` in the root of the working copy. (A `make.bat` is supplied
for Windows, which will run the supplied copy of GNU Make.)

The output ROM images are in the `.build` folder in the working copy:

- `exmon2.rom` is for the BBC B/B+/Master
- `exmon2e.rom` is for the Electron

## Using the ROMs on your BBC or emulator

The .rom files are ordinary 16 KB ROM images. Transfer them to your
BBC, use them to program a PROM, load them into an emulator.

If you use [BeebLink](https://github.com/tom-seddon/beeblink/), add
`beeb` in the working copy to your BeebLink search path. You'll get a
volume called `exmon2_build` containing `:Z.R.EXMON2` (BBC B/B+/Master
version) and `:Z.R.EXMON2E` (Electron version).

# Building an original copy

Check out any of the following tags to build the corresponding
version. You'll need a POSIX-type system with the usual POSIX-type
stuff installed, along with
[64tass](https://sourceforge.net/projects/tass64/) on the path.
(Building these on Windows is an exercise for the reader. Sorry!)

The resulting ROM in each case is `.build/exmon2.rom`.

These ROMs are not Electron-compatible, though some stuff will work to
an extent.

## v2.02

Looks to be the newest version I've found so far. Probably
recommended.

## v2.02-alt

Doesn't properly support BBC B/B+ with a 65c02. It will assume your
BBC has an ordinary non-CMOS 6502.

## v2.01

All the problems of v2.02, and it doesn't support BASIC 4r32 either.

(Also a few code differences that I haven't looked at very closely -
looks like there may be some issues with running code in other ROMs.)

# ali_baba_reveng
Reverse engineering of Ali Baba for the Apple II (1982)

[main.pdf](main.pdf) is the literate programming document for this project. This means the explanatory text is interspersed with source code. The source code can be extracted from the document and compiled.

The goal is to provide all the source code necessary to reproduce a binary identical to the one found on the Internet Archive's [Lode_Runner_1983_Broderbund_cr_Reset_Vector.do](https://archive.org/details/a2_Lode_Runner_1983_Broderbund_cr_Reset_Vector) disk image.

The assembly code is assembled using [`dasm`](https://dasm-assembler.github.io/).

This document doesn't explain every last detail. It's assumed that the reader can find enough details on the 6502 processor and the Apple II series of computers to fill in the gaps.

## Useful 6502 and Apple II resources:

* [Beneath Apple DOS](https://archive.org/details/beneath-apple-dos), by Don Worth and Pieter Lechner, 1982.
* [Apple II Computer Graphics](https://archive.org/details/williams-et-al-1983-apple-ii-computer-graphics), by Ken Williams, Bob Kernaghan, and Lisa Kernaghan, 1983.
* [6502 Assembly Language Programming](https://archive.org/details/6502alp), by Lance A. Leventhal, 1979.
* [Beagle Bros Apple Colors and ASCII Values](https://archive.org/details/Beagle_Bros-Poster_1), Beagle Bros Micro Software Inc, 1984.
* [Hi-Res Graphics and Animation Using Assembly Language, The Guide for Apple II Programmers](https://archive.org/details/hi-res-graphics-and-animation-using-assembly-language), by Leanard I. Malkin, 1985.

## Compilation

This step should not be necessary, as the release provides the assembly files, the 6502 binary, and the PDF.

### Prerequisites

* [`dasm`](https://dasm-assembler.github.io/), the 6502 assembler.
* A distribution of [TeX Live](https://www.tug.org/texlive/) with the `booktabs` and `tikz` packages.
* [`noweb`](https://github.com/nrnrnr/noweb)

To compile `main.nw`, you must use the `noweb` package and a `TeX` distribution such as TeX Live.

WARNING: The latest TeX Live, 2022, is known to break `noweb` [[bug](https://github.com/nrnrnr/noweb/issues/24)]. Use TeXLive 2021 or earlier until the bug is fixed.

### Generating the PDF

```sh
$ noweave -delay -index main.nw > main.tex
$ pdflatex main.tex
$ pdflatex main.tex
```

Yes, you have to run `pdflatex` twice. The first run generates auxilliary information about indexes that the second run can use to properly cross-reference things.

### Generating the binary

First, you must place the filter script `ignore_preuse_text.py` in `/usr/lib/noweb`. Sorry Windows users, I don't know where to put your filter scripts.

The `ignore_preuse_text.py` filter makes it so that uses of code blocks do not get extra indentation when that use is indented. This is important for the assembly language output, and makes the PDF output more pleasant to read.

```sh
$ notangle -filter ignore_preuse_text.py main.nw > main2.asm
$ python3 reorder_asm.py main2.asm > main.asm
$ dasm main.asm -f3 -omain.bin
```

`reorder_asm.py` reads the `main.asm` output, and reorders code blocks so that
their ORG locations are increasing. This is necessary because `dasm` doesn't handle
code blocks whose origins jump around.

# Panzer Dragoon Saga Decompilation

A full decompilation and modern reimplementation of **Panzer Dragoon Saga** (Sega Saturn, 1998, Team Andromeda). This is a legacy version. New one is here: https://github.com/blythos/atolm


The goal is a native modern port: an application that loads the original disc image and runs the complete game on modern hardware — not emulation, but a true reimplementation of the game engine and logic.

## Status

**Phase 1: Asset Pipeline** — in progress. See [PROGRESS.md](docs/PROGRESS.md) for detailed status.

### What works today

| Category | Status |
|----------|--------|
| **3D Models** | ✅ All 351 MCB/CGB pairs extractable — dragons, characters, NPCs, enemies, bosses, fields |
| **Textures** | ✅ LUT (mode 1) and RGB555 (mode 5) fully decoded; bank-mode (0, 4) renders as greyscale pending PNB parser |
| **Skeleton & Animation** | ✅ Hierarchical poses and keyframe animation playback (4 animation modes) |
| **FMV Video** | ✅ All 14 CPK Cinepak videos extracted to MP4 with frame-accurate subtitles |
| **Sequenced Music** | ✅ 86 SEQ→MIDI conversions; 89 BIN tone banks→WAV instrument samples; official track names from SNDTEST.PRG |
| **PCM Audio** | ⬜ 270 PCM files on disc — extractor not yet started |
| **2D Assets** | 🔄 PNB extracted (raw + visualisations); SCB parser not yet started |
| **Fonts** | ✅ All 65 FNT files extracted — 16×16 1bpp glyph bitmaps → PNG sprite sheets + JSON |
| **3D Viewer** | ✅ Browser-based Three.js viewer with textured models, animation playback, and asset browser |
| **Sound Test** | ✅ Browser-based MIDI playback + WAV auditioning with search and filtering |

## What This Is

This project converts the original SH-2 machine code and binary data formats into documented, readable source code. It builds on [yaz0r's Azel project](https://github.com/yaz0r/Azel) — an extraordinary MIT-licenced partial decompilation representing 5+ years of reverse engineering work.

Three reinforcing tracks:
- **Asset extraction** — parse every binary format (models, textures, audio, video, text)
- **Code decompilation** — convert SH-2 assembly to C/C++ for every game subsystem
- **Reimplementation** — modern engine (SDL2 + modern renderer) that runs the decompiled logic

## Legal

**This project does not contain any game data.** You must provide your own legally obtained copy of Panzer Dragoon Saga. The reimplementation loads the original disc image at runtime, the same way an emulator does.

Panzer Dragoon Saga is © SEGA. This is a clean-room style decompilation for interoperability and preservation purposes.

## Repository Structure

```
atolm/
├── docs/                           # Project documentation
│   ├── PROJECT_SCOPE.md            # Full scope, architecture, development phases
│   ├── PROGRESS.md                 # What's done, what's next
│   ├── TECHNICAL_REFERENCE.md      # Binary format specifications
│   ├── TOOL_CHAIN_AND_ROADMAP.md   # Tool inventory and path to playability
│   ├── QUICK_REFERENCE.md          # Cheat sheet for common operations
│   ├── SESSION_LOG.md              # Development history
│   └── cpk_format_research.md      # Sega FILM / CPK container format notes
│
├── tools/                          # Python extraction and analysis tools
│   ├── common/                     # Shared modules
│   │   ├── iso9660.py              #   ISO9660 disc image reader
│   │   └── saturn.py               #   Saturn hardware utilities
│   │
│   │  ── 3D Model Pipeline ──
│   ├── pds_extract.py              # MCB/CGB → JSON + texture atlas (main extractor)
│   ├── pds_extract_raw.py          # Raw binary MCB/CGB extraction
│   ├── mcb_extract.py              # MCB/CGB → glTF (.glb) export
│   │
│   │  ── 3D Viewer ──
│   ├── pds_viewer.html             # Browser-based model viewer (Three.js)
│   ├── viewer_renderer.js          # Viewer rendering engine
│   ├── viewer_animation.js         # Saturn animation state machine port
│   │
│   │  ── FMV / Subtitle Pipeline ──
│   ├── cpk_extract.py              # Sega FILM CPK → MP4 + WAV
│   ├── extract_subtitles.py        # PRG bytecode → SRT subtitles
│   ├── batch_process_FMVs.py       # Batch extract + subtitle + mux pipeline
│   │
│   │  ── Audio / Music ──
│   ├── seq_extract.py              # Extract SEQ/BIN files from disc
│   ├── seq_to_midi.py              # SEQ → MIDI converter
│   ├── ton_to_wav.py               # BIN tone bank → WAV instrument samples
│   ├── snd_split.py                # SEQ↔BIN pair catalogue (all 4 discs)
│   ├── build_sound_catalogue.py    # SNDTEST.PRG → official track names
│   ├── make_sf2.py                 # SoundFont (SF2) builder
│   ├── pcm_extract.py              # PCM audio extractor (WIP)
│   │
│   │  ── 2D Assets ──
│   ├── pnb_extract.py              # PNB pattern name extraction
│   ├── fnt_extract.py              # FNT font glyph extraction
│   │
│   │  ── Sound Test ──
│   ├── sound_test_server.py        # HTTP server for browser sound test
│   ├── sound_test.html             # Browser-based sound test UI
│   │
│   │  ── Debug / Analysis ──
│   ├── debug/                      # Diagnostic and inspection scripts
│   │   ├── inspect_iso.py          #   List all files on a disc image
│   │   ├── audit_fmv_durations.py  #   Check subtitle/video sync
│   │   ├── compare_discs.py        #   Cross-disc file comparison
│   │   ├── inspect_movie_dat.py    #   Dump MOVIE.DAT contents
│   │   ├── inspect_movie_prg.py    #   Dump MOVIE.PRG contents
│   │   ├── inspect_verts.py        #   Vertex data inspector
│   │   ├── check_scale.py          #   Model scale validator
│   │   └── sim_mode4.py            #   Animation mode 4 simulator
│   └── investigate_bin.py          # BIN format investigation helper
│
├── tests/                          # Validation tests (planned)
├── output/                         # Extracted assets (gitignored)
├── ISOs/                           # Disc images (gitignored)
├── LICENSE                         # MIT
└── README.md                       # This file
```

## Getting Started

### Requirements
- Python 3.6+ (most tools use pure stdlib — no dependencies)
- [FFmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/) for video muxing (`cpk_extract.py`, `batch_process_FMVs.py`)
- A modern browser with WebGL for the 3D viewer and sound test
- A Panzer Dragoon Saga disc image (raw Mode 2 track, `.bin` format)

### Extract 3D models
```bash
# Extract all models from Disc 1
python tools/pds_extract.py "path/to/disc1.bin" --extract-all -o output/

# Serve the viewer
cd output/
copy ..\tools\pds_viewer.html .
copy ..\tools\viewer_renderer.js .
copy ..\tools\viewer_animation.js .
python -m http.server 8080
# Open http://localhost:8080/pds_viewer.html
```

### Extract FMVs with subtitles
```bash
python tools/batch_process_FMVs.py "path/to/disc1.bin"
```

### Extract music
```bash
# Extract all SEQ/BIN files
python tools/seq_extract.py --iso "path/to/disc1.bin" --extract --output output/seq_extract/

# Convert a track to MIDI
python tools/seq_to_midi.py --input output/seq_extract/raw/KOGATA.SEQ --output output/midi/KOGATA.mid

# Extract instrument samples from a tone bank
python tools/ton_to_wav.py --input output/seq_extract/raw/KOGATA.BIN --output output/ton_wav/KOGATA/
```

See [tools/README.md](tools/README.md) for full documentation of all tools.

## Acknowledgements

- **yaz0r** — [Azel project](https://github.com/yaz0r/Azel). The foundation of this work. 468 commits and 76,000+ lines of decompiled PDS engine code, open-sourced under MIT licence.
- **Team Andromeda** — for creating one of the most remarkable games ever made.
- **The Panzer Dragoon community** — [Panzer Dragoon Legacy](https://www.panzerdragoonlegacy.com/), [Will of the Ancients](https://www.willoftheancients.com/) — decades of keeping the flame alive.

A completely client-side retro-computing tool optimized for modern browsers. This single-file web application allows you to convert images, write native Sinclair BASIC, compile `.TAP` files, and synthesize real-time cassette loading audio directly in your browser.

# d71/d81writer
A 1541 Ultimate 2 write tool
============================

Written by Ernoman and WdW.

![writer](https://github.com/wiebow/d81writer/blob/master/images/screen.png)

Introduction
============

This C64 tool will enable you to use your 1541 Ultimate 2 cartridge (U2) to
write .D71 and .D81 images to a physical drive.

The C64 version uses the standard kernal calls, so operation is slow. A C128
version using burst write commands is in the works.

Preparations
============

Set your physical drive to another id than the emulated U2 drive, because having
two drives with the same device id on the serial bus is asking for trouble.

The diskette must be formatted before you can use it. It does not need
to be empty.  In order to get a 1:1 copy it's best to format the diskette with
the index option, as the copy tool will not write empty sectors.

Enther the U2 cartridge and enable the command interface and the REU with at
least 1MB of memory.

Disable any cartridge in the U2 interface. Some cartridges, like the Retro
Replay, do not play nice and will cause the command interface to fail.

On a C128 in C64 mode: When running the program on a C128 (in C64 mode) you
need to modify the 1541U2 option CPU addr valid after PHI2 to 100ns.

Put your image files somewhere on a USB or Micro SD card and insert it into the
U2.

When the tools starts, make sure if you see the ultimate dos version appear
under the header. If this does not happen, re-check your U2 settings!! The tool
will not function properly until you see the dos version.

Usage
=====

1) Enter the type of image you want to write.
2) Enter the path to the folder containing the images files.
3) Type in the name of the image file.
4) Enter the destination drive device ID and watch the counter until it reaches
   track 80 (for a D81 image) or 70 (for a D71 image)
